articles.title: Man Utd's Mauricio Pochettino pursuit and Michael Carrick decisions
articles.text:
Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.

Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.

But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.

On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.

A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.

It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.

What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.

By that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.

There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.

But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.

Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth, United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.

It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.

There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.

Carrick has conducted himself with great dignity during the turmoil of the past few days and he leaves the club - certainly in the eyes of supporters - with his standing as a United great intact.

When United first appointed Carrick - initially on an interim basis following the sacking of Ruben Amorim in January - he had a positive impact on the squad, and subsequently results.

United liked his positive messaging to the players and media. They felt Carrick brought calm to rocky waters and protected his players at every opportunity - a contrast from at least the closing stages of Amorim's tenure.

On the pitch, the United hierarchy felt Carrick's style of play allowed the forward players more freedom, and they won 12 of their last 17 matches of the season.

While United considered other managerial options in the summer, there was ultimately a sense Carrick had earned a shot at the job on a permanent basis.

The 45-year-old signed a two-year deal, though it is understood United contractually protected themselves in the event of an early termination.

Part of the thought process was to provide the players with some managerial stability given the increased turnover of head coaches in recent years.

Yet the season started poorly with defeat at newly promoted Hull City - and has only spiralled downward since.

United are third bottom of the Premier League and 17th in the Champions League table.

articles.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.text:
Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer.

The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.

However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £11m today from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer.

Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business".

Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC that he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street".

"They refused to prioritise protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he said.

"It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge."

Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year".

He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now".

"It's a good business, it's a much-loved business and, particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added.

articles.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
articles.text:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.

The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".

Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.

A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century
articles.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.

Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith, who received 48.7%, congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

The contest was not considered to be in play until the final weeks of the campaign, given President Donald Trump won the state in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.

Colom offered a victory speech on the campus of Tougaloo College, met by hundreds of cheering supporters standing side-by-side under the night sky.

Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election.

"They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," Colom said.

"It's not something that I did y'all," he continued. "It's something we did."

"In Mississippi, it's local people that make the difference."

Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.

The room burst into deafening applause and cheers.

"This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board.

"This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising.

"This is a historic election."

Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.

"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."

The last black senator in the state before Colom was Bruce who was chosen by the state legislature.

It has taken a century and a half for the state to choose a new one, this time by Mississippi voters.

In his campaign, Colom strove to engage Republican voters, even going to a Trump rally to speak to people in line outside.

Another key moment was his opponent telling voters to "pick another protein" when asked about surging beef prices, something Colom turned into a viral advert of his own., external

articles.title: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
articles.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.

It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".

Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth.

It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.

The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.

The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.

Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.

This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.

While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either.

Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helping to boost growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes.

While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week.

Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment.

I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss.

However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year.

Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again.

There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed.

The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf.

Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too.

Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy".

articles.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
articles.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

articles.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
articles.text:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times,, external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

In his interim report,, external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around.

"What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC.

"Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added.

But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants.

articles.title: Anthropic set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning
articles.text:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.

It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.

The huge valuation comes despite the company warning last month that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

It is floating at a volatile time for big tech firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.

There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.

In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.

However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".

She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."

Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT on 19 November, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.

articles.title: Tinned food and bottled water sales jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.text:
Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.

Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
articles.text:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

"It is really interesting to see this kind of backlash," said Kate Vlietstra, senior director of food and drink at market research analyst Mintel.

"It is something we have been seeing a bit more in recent years, particularly with the trend for unboxing on social media," she said,

"It means that, inevitably, if people are not feeling they're getting the value that they have hoped for from the advent calendar...they've purchased, then yes, there is going to be a backlash."

Advent calendars remain popular, according to Helen Wing, head of innovation at market research company Ipsos though she said that "the buzz around them has reduced a little bit".

She said according to Ipsos research, people are willing to pay a bit more for an advent calendar but the contents have to justify the price tag.

Using a £285 advent calendar sold by Liberty as an example, Wing said the upmarket department story is "very open about the value of the contents".

"They will say there is over £1,000 worth of content," she said. "If you've got that reassurance when you're making the purchase, particularly if it is for a gift, then it is important to have some faith that the contents are actually going to be worth the money that you're paying."

articles.title: US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices
articles.text:
US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.

Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.

However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.

The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.

However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.

While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.

For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.

The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.

When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.

While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.

Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.

Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

articles.title: Live Updates: Jensen Huang Resigns From Nvidia After Affairs
articles.text:
Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, Nvidia’s 10-member board said in a statement.

Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of artificial intelligence projects. Mr. Huang’s exit, which followed a lengthy board meeting on Wednesday, will have widespread ripple effects. Shares of Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable public companies, plunged at the start of trading, weighing on the broader market.

Nvidia, long a maker of graphics chips, became a linchpin of A.I. development in recent years, which put it at the center of the U.S.-China tussle for dominance in the sector.

A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang, 63, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who goes by Alice Huang, who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang. The Times also reported that Mr. Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action.

U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped smuggle restricted chips into China. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment, and China has rejected the espionage claims and called the smuggling allegations “smears.”

Nvidia’s board, which has had a long track record of deference to its chief executive, did not mention Mr. Huang’s conduct in its statement. It called his contributions to Nvidia “profound” and thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”

While the board begins its search for the company’s next leader, Mr. Trump had his own idea: Tim Cook, the former chief executive of Apple. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote on social media.

Here’s what else to know:

Another affair: Mr. Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. He is the latest member to join a growing club of chief executives brought down by affairs.

A long-term strategy: China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people. Although the use of seduction in espionage is not unique to China, the country’s use of it differs in the amount of time it is willing to invest. Read more ›

Economic fallout: Mr. Huang’s departure could affect the economy more broadly than a typical C.E.O. departure. He ran Nvidia almost single-handedly and was unusually central to its success. Nvidia, in turn, has been unusually central to the artificial intelligence boom, a crucial driver of U.S. economic growth while some other sectors have been struggling. Read more ›

Huang and Trump: Few tech executives have had as much sway with Mr. Trump, who has called Mr. Huang an “honorable man” and said he believed that Mr. Huang was not aware that he had been involved with a Chinese spy. The president is scheduled to travel to China next week, and he said on Monday that he did not plan to bring up the Nvidia matter in talks with China’s leader, Xi Jinping.

The fate of the foundation, which the couple started in 2007 and oversee together, is not clear.

Ms. Huang is the foundation’s president, and Mr. Huang is its secretary and chief financial officer, according to the most recent tax return for the charitable organization, which is called the Jen-hsun & Lori Huang Foundation. In 2024, its most recent tax year on file, the foundation’s assets nearly tripled, thanks to more than $5 billion in investment gains.

Marital issues have led to major shifts in the world of philanthropy in recent years, such as the departure by Melinda French Gates from her joint charitable entity with her ex-husband, Bill, and the elevation of MacKenzie Scott as one of America’s biggest givers following her divorce from Jeff Bezos.

The Huangs’ foundation is rather low-profile: Despite being one of America’s biggest charitable entities, it has no website or lists any public staff.

And the couple had only just begun giving. The biggest public gifts by the Huangs have gone to higher-education institutions, a relatively safe and conventional place to disburse large amounts of money. They have announced a combined $180 million or so to four schools, including a $75 million donation in July to establish an art and design college at Vanderbilt University’s planned outpost in San Francisco.

Mr. Huang has described his philanthropic giving as an investment, not charity. “I don’t give anything away,” he said in 2010, dismissing the premise of the question. “The way I think about it is I’m investing in the next generation, to help us and to inspire us to create even better and more useful technologies.”

Their giving has also intersected with what is good for Nvidia. The Huangs’ foundation bought computing time from Coreweave, a key Nvidia partner and customer, and donated $108.3 million of it to universities and other nonprofits, according to an Nvidia corporate filing in May.

Posing a risk to national security is not the usual reason for ousting a chief executive. More often, it is that a relationship was in violation of company policy.

Large companies generally have had policies that prohibit managers and direct reports from having romantic relationships. Nvidia’s code of conduct tells employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.”

“When it comes to direct reports, companies have had hard policies and have had for ages,” said Charles G. Tharp, executive vice president of the CHRO Association, a group for human resources officers.

Mark Hurd, who had helped build HP into a powerhouse tech company, was fired in 2010 after its board found that he’d failed to disclose use of company funds, and that he’d had a “close personal relationship” with a contractor. In 2018, Brian Krzanich resigned from Intel after the chip company learned of a “past consensual relationship” the chief executive had with an employee.

Tech is not the only industry to be hit by scandal. Last year, Ashley Buchanan was fired as chief executive of Kohl’s, the department store chain, after the company learned that he was trying to direct business to a vendor who turned out to be his romantic partner. Mr. Buchanan was in the role for just a few months. Rodney McMullen, the chief executive of the grocery chain Kroger, resigned last year after an investigation by its board found that his personal conduct was inconsistent with the company’s policies.

McDonald’s went through an unusually public yearslong battle starting in 2019. That year, the company fired Steve Easterbrook, its chief executive, after its board learned he had engaged in a consensual relationship with a subordinate that violated company policy. Eight months later, another McDonald’s employee reported a previous sexual relationship with Mr. Easterbrook. McDonald’s then sued Mr. Easterbrook, accusing him of lying and concealing multiple relationships with McDonald’s employees. The case was settled, and Mr. Easterbrook apologized and gave back more than $105 million in cash and stock to the company.

Companies likely tightened enforcement on policies on bosses being in relationships with subordinates during the #MeToo era, which saw accusations of sexual harassment and coercion, said Mr. Tharp. In 2018, Leslie Moonves, the longtime chief executive of the CBS Corporation, was one of the most high-profile entertainment figures to be ousted from his position during the #MeToo era. He stepped down after several women accused him of sexual harassment. Mr. Moonves received no severance package.

In the wake of Mr. Moonves’s ouster, the board of CBS also named six new members.

Boards of directors are responsible for monitoring the conduct of their chief executives and ultimately decide if a chief executive needs to step down.

Founders of very successful companies — like Mr. Huang — are often treated with deference by their boards. “They are in awe of their founder for very good reasons,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor of leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the author of “The Hero’s Farewell.”

In Nvidia’s case, he said, “the board has done the right thing, but it has taken too long.”

“There were lots of indicators for any board paying attention,” he added.

Other founders have been fired because of their temperament or management style and later ended up returning to the companies they built. In 1985, Steve Jobs was forced out of Apple after an internal power struggle and a disastrous rollout of new technology. In 2000, he returned and had a legendary run as Apple’s chief executive. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, had a shorter time away from his artificial-intelligence empire. He was pushed out by the board of directors on a Friday afternoon in 2023. Five days later, he was reinstated as the company’s leader after allies, including fellow Silicon Valley executives, employees and investors, urged his return.

Here’s how the events unfolded.

2023: A Chinese executive named Alice Huang sets up a data firm in Singapore called Megaspeed. The company, which originally had Chinese owners, would soon buy billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips. In May 2023, Nvidia reaches $1 trillion in value.

December 2023: While it’s not clear when Mr. Huang, who is married, met Ms. Huang, they were acquainted by December 2023, when they had dinner with colleagues at a restaurant in Singapore. In June 2024, they were seen socializing at an event in Taipei, Taiwan.

June 2024 to June 2025: A Megaspeed subsidiary receives more than 200 shipments of Nvidia A.I. equipment.

Early 2025: Weeks after Mr. Trump begins his second term, Mr. Huang visits the White House to meet with him for the first time.

March 2025: Ms. Huang visits Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.

April 2025: During a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago, Mr. Huang makes a case to Mr. Trump for allowing chip companies like Nvidia to do business with China. The same month, the White House shuts down Nvidia’s sales to China, strengthening Biden-era regulations that put limits on the sale of A.I. technology.

May 2025: Ms. Huang and Mr. Huang dine with others in Taipei. They pose for a photo together, and she kisses him on the cheek.

July 2025: Nvidia becomes the first public company ever to be worth $4 trillion. The Trump administration reverses course and assures Nvidia that it will be granted a license to sell certain chips to China.

September 2025: The U.S. government, through the Commerce Department, begins an investigation into Megaspeed, examining whether some of the Nvidia chips it bought were sent to China, a possible violation of U.S. export controls.

October 2025: U.S. intelligence officials tell Mr. Trump that Mr. Huang has a relationship with Ms. Huang, whom they describe as a Chinese intelligence asset. Mr. Trump chooses not to take any action.

December 2025: Mr. Trump approves the sale of more powerful Nvidia chips to China.

May 2026: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns U.S. officials that Mr. Huang is in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. The same month, Mr. Trump invites Mr. Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing.

October 2026: Mr. Huang’s affair with Ms. Huang is reported in The New York Times.

November 2026: After Mr. Huang admits the affair, Nvidia’s board says it will conduct an investigation. The New York Times later reports that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports to him. On Nov. 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announces that Mr. Huang has resigned.

In a note to Nvidia’s employees, Ms. Kress said she believed “deeply in this company” and called its employees “our greatest strength.” She said Nvidia would have a companywide meeting on Nov. 18 to discuss its future.

She will remain Nvidia’s chief financial officer while serving as its interim chief executive officer until the board names a permanent successor. The board said on Thursday that it had started a search for that replacement and would consider internal and external candidates. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, is leading the company as it enters an uncertain next chapter. Under the leadership of Mr. Huang, Nvidia grew from a niche maker of computer chips used for video games to one of the most valuable public companies in the world and the linchpin of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

Ms. Kress, 59, faces a challenging road. She is temporarily taking over a company that has been tightly controlled by her predecessor. Mr. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and had managed all aspects of its business with a flat structure that placed him at the center of its day-to-day operations.

His family members had steadily risen through its ranks in recent years. And while Ms. Kress is already familiar to Wall Street, she does not have Mr. Huang’s relationships with Nvidia’s sprawling supply chain or Washington.

Ms. Kress has a bachelor’s degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a master’s degree in business administration from Southern Methodist University. She previously worked in finance at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco, before joining Nvidia in 2013.

Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Ms. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role.

“I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Huang said on a podcast this year.

As chief financial officer, Ms. Kress was responsible for communicating with Nvidia’s investors and Wall Street. Over the past four years, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message on quarterly earnings calls as Nvidia’s revenue and profits soared, though she also expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict the sale of advanced chips to China.

In 2013, Nvidia’s revenue was $4.28 billion. Its revenue in its most recent fiscal year was more than 50 times that, at nearly $215.94 billion. In August, Ms. Kress told analysts and investors that Nvidia expects to grow 70 percent next year.

Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price in recent years. As of March, she owned more than 4.4 million shares in the company, according to its most recent annual report, a stake that was worth about $780.4 million at the time. That makes Ms. Kress one of the largest individual shareholders of Nvidia. Its largest individual shareholder, with a 3.56 percent stake, is Mr. Huang.

Ms. Kress’s transition — as well as that of the permanent successor to Mr. Huang — could be complicated by how Mr. Huang managed Nvidia. He led the company with an executive team of more than 60 people who directly reported to him, many of whom are longtime loyalists. That flat structure will be difficult to unwind. On a podcast in January, Mr. Huang described his executive team as a group of “60 people who could be world-class C.E.O.s for many other companies.”

For the time being, Ms. Kress will be C.E.O. for Nvidia.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to testify to US Congress amid scandal, reports say, as CFO Colette Kress replaces him as interim CEO – follow live
articles.text:
Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO - at a glance

Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee, bookending a stunning fall from grace of one of the leading figures of the AI boom. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named.

Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 13% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced and ricocheted through the global economy. After a partial rebound, they were down 7% in morning trading, wiping more than $320bn (£242bn) off Nvidia’s value on the day and more than $600bn for the week – valuing the company at about $3.9tn.

A statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded. “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said. It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Nvidia’s board directors said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.

In the US, the Democratic House minority leader – expected to become speaker in the next Congress – Hakeem Jeffries said lawmakers should receive a classified briefing on the scandal. “We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation and to the extent that our national security has been compromised,” Jeffries said at his ongoing press conference. “The American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”

Updated at 12.46 EST

double quotation markHalf the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

Options traders cashed in parts of their bets against Nvidia and positioned for a longer-term share ⁠price recovery on Thursday, after CEO Jensen Huang announced he was stepping down.

“Nvida’s competitive ⁠advantage and customers don’t disappear overnight,” said Seth Hickle, chief investment officer at Mindset Wealth Management.

“The market ​is trying to determine whether this is a ‌temporary leadership crisis or ‌something that fundamentally changes the AI investment thesis.“

Options give holders the right, but not the obligation, ‌to buy or sell the underlying stock at a set price before a certain date.

Senior White ⁠House officials are discussing whether the commerce secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out ⁠in the wake ⁠of ​the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now former CEO Jensen Huang, sources told Reuters.

A growing number of lawmakers criticised Lutnick over ⁠the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese ​companies to a key ‌US trade blacklist, ‌and over whether the government was properly overseeing ‌Nvidia’s exports to China.

The criticism predates Thursday’s resignation of Nvidia’s Huang, who announced he would step down as CEO of the leading AI chipmaker after revelations of an affair with ‌Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

A ​White House official said president Donald ​Trump “maintains ​complete confidence in the secretary [Lutnick] and his ability to carry out the position.“

Over in Washington DC, the US Senate’s Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, has called for an investigation both into former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese spy, and the Trump administration’s handling of the matter.

The White House reportedly knew about Huang’s involvement with a woman said to be linked to Chinese intelligence, but still let him accompany Donald Trump on an official visit to China.

Here’s what Schumer – who may be the Senate majority leader in about two months – had to say about all that:

Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk.

The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?

Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.

It comes not long after Schumer’s House counterpart, Hakeem Jeffries, said lawmakers should receive a classified briefing on the scandal.

The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said. It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Nvidia’s board directors said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.

In the US, the Democratic House minority leader – expected to become speaker in the next Congress – Hakeem Jeffries said lawmakers should receive a classified briefing on the scandal. “We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation and to the extent that our national security has been compromised,” Jeffries said at his ongoing press conference. “The American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”

Updated at 12.46 EST

From washing dishes at Denny’s to rockstar of AI: the rise and fall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang wasn’t always in his trademark leather jacket. When the multibillionaire, now former Nvidia chief executive was a teenager in the US, his first job was waiting tables and washing dishes at a branch of Denny’s.

“It teaches you humility, it teaches you hard work, it teaches you hospitality,” he said in 2023 of his time at the diner chain.

Decades later, having become one of the richest people on the planet, Huang put on a Denny’s apron in tribute to his former employer at an Nvidia event in 2025.

By this point Huang had become a rockstar of the artificial intelligence boom – befitting his signature item of clothing – feted around the world by investors, fellow tech executives and politicians.

The company that Huang co-founded makes the computer chips that are integral to the development and operation of AI systems such as ChatGPT.

Demand for Nvidia’s products has surged as hundreds of billions of dollars have been poured into a technology that, according to its many boosters, will transform the global economy. The crude analogy is that Huang and Nvidia have become the main purveyors of shovels in the AI gold rush.

In technical jargon, its AI chips are known as graphics processor units (GPUs), which were originally designed to handle the graphics for video games. But it turned out that a GPU’s ability to carry out masses of technical calculations simultaneously and quickly is very handy for developing and operating AI systems, which have a voracious appetite for data crunching.

Nvidia is also very good at creating networks of its chips, which produces the computing power artificial intelligence needs, and provides the CUDA software that helps the company’s GPUs perform so well for AI customers.

Jen-Hsun Huang, 63, was born in Taiwan to a chemical engineer father and a schoolteacher mother. Decades later, the island would become the epicentre of chip manufacturing and the foundry for Nvidia’s highly advanced chips.

Also in DC, the Democratic House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries said lawmakers should receive a classified briefing on the scandal surrounding chipmaker Nvidia.

The company is seen as among America’s most important, because it makes advanced chips that are powering the AI boom.

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation and to the extent that our national security has been compromised,” Jeffries said at his ongoing press conference.

“The American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”

Bloomberg’s chief political correspondent is reporting that the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving.

In an X post, Annmarie Hordern said:

double quotation markHouse Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast told reporters Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving.

For the time being at least though, Colette Kress is stepping up as the company’s interim CEO.

So what do we know about the former CFO?

Well, in her CFO role, Kress was a key architect for financing deals with many of the Nvidia’s biggest customers - which today include the likes of other AI titans, such as Anthropic and CoreWeave.

Kress has a long resume in the tech world. Prior to joining Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments in a variety of roles, according to her executive bio on the company’s website.

Trump says former Apple CEO Cook should replace Huang at Nvidia

US president Donald ⁠Trump said on Thursday that former Apple chief executive ⁠Tim Cook should ⁠replace ​Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia.

“NOW THAT Nvidia ⁠CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there ⁠is only one man to take ​his place - ‌TIM COOK of Apple,” ‌Trump said on social media. “A Legend ‌replaces a Legend!” he added.

Cook stepped down after a 15-year stint as Apple’s CEO in September and is now executive chairman at the iPhone-maker.

Meanwhile, Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, has said that investors have been left “concerned” over the change of leadership at Nvidia.

She said that although the interim appointment of Colette Kress will “provide continuity” for the firm, it remains to be seen if Nvidia will be able to keep pace with its rivals.

double quotation markThe main concern for investors is the uncertainty following a change of leadership, especially one with a lack of planning like this one. However, the key-man risk is significant, but it shouldn’t be confused with the company’s entire investment case.

Huang has been instrumental in Nvidia’s transformation into the dominant supplier of AI computing infrastructure, and his departure creates uncertainty around strategy, execution and relationships with major customers. But Nvidia’s technological advantages, CUDA software ecosystem and substantial order book do not disappear with its CEO.

The appointment of CFO Colette Kress provides some continuity, although investors will want reassurance that the broader leadership team can maintain Nvidia’s pace of innovation and defend its market position.

She added that Nvidia’s recovery today “looks partly driven by bargain hunting after an aggressive selloff, with some investors seemingly betting that Nvidia’s competitive advantages, strong AI demand and established customer relationships will survive a leadership transition.”

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at the the UK’s largest non-advisory investment service Wealth Club, said Nvidia’s board “clearly wanted to disassociate with Jensen Huang”.

In analysis earlier today, she said:

double quotation markEven Jensen Huang’s superstar status could not eclipse the deep damage the scandal has wreaked on the Nvidia’s reputation. Even tech icons of his stature are not immune to being acountable to corporate responsibility.

The emergence of the second affair, this one rumoured to be with an employee, appears to have been the last straw for the board.

With the firm facing so many investigations – launched by the FBI and from Capitol hill, the board clearly wants to disassociate the company from Huang’s actions as much as possible.

Streeter added that interim CEO Colette Kress is “seen as a safe pair of hands” and that she has “clearly been brought in to steady the ship”.

However, she warned:

double quotation markBut she lacks global status and is unlikely to be able to forge such deep global commercial ties as Nvidia is set to enter into a period of uncertainty over strategic priorities, pricing, supply agreements and future product commitments.

Nvidia has lost a strategic visionary, and it’s set to have repercussions right through the AI trade, given how the chip giant is right at the heart of this technological revolution.

Updated at 10.16 EST

articles.title: College students rally in support of Starbucks baristas urging boycott over contract impasse
articles.text:
Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at over 40 college campuses across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United boycott campaign as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.

Starbucks Workers United is seeking better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store. It has called on the public to boycott Starbucks until its first contract is reached.

More than 700 Starbucks stores have voted to unionize, representing more than 12,000 baristas. It typically takes over 450 days for a new labor union to negotiate and reach its first contract, but it has been nearly five years since the first Starbucks store in Buffalo, New York, voted to unionize in December 2021.

Starbucks Workers United began to focus on college campuses in 2023, calling on campuses to cancel their contracts with Starbucks in protest against the company’s response to union-organizing efforts. In response, Cornell University and Pomona College did not renew their contracts with the company, while UCLA stopped offering Starbucks products in their cafes.

Rallies and events will take place at private and public universities across the country, including the University of Pennsylvania, Northwestern and the University of Washington.

The union push come ahead of the company’s busy holiday season, including Starbucks’ Red Cup Day on 17 November, when customers receive a reusable holiday cup.

“Starbucks has been fueling the working class for decades, but they’re failing the workers that fuel their profits,” said Andrew Trinklein, a barista who is participating in an event at the University of Texas at Austin. “We’re really trying to push and get support from college campus students… in joining the boycott.”

His store recently unionized, and he expressed shock at how the company hired pricey union avoidance consultants in attempts to deter workers from unionizing. Starbucks has reportedly spent tens of millions of dollars related to union avoidance, though it has not disclosed the full costs relating to its union-organizing efforts.

Trinklein emphasized that employees are currently employed at-will, meaning they have no just-cause job security protections.

“Right now it’s just a toss-up whether we have a job tomorrow or not. Say they don’t like something that we’re doing – say we don’t write on a cup. We could be fired for it tomorrow,” Trinklein said, referring to the company’s policy requiring employees to write friendly messages on cups for customers. “But with this contract, that won’t be possible. We’ll have protections from stuff like that.”

Efforts to pressure Starbucks to negotiate were temporarily paused when the union and Starbucks reached an agreement on a path forward in February 2024. But negotiations broke down shortly after Brian Niccol took over as Starbucks CEO.

Niccol previously served as CEO of Chipotle from 2018 to 2024, and under his tenure, the company agreed to pay $240,000 to former workers as part of a settlement over a store closing in Maine after it unionized, which the National Labor Relations Board said was illegal. Chipotle has denied wrongdoing.

In recent years, Starbucks has been found to have violated federal labor law by the NLRB in several cases regarding its responses to union-organizing efforts. Starbucks has challenged these rulings.

In a statement, a Starbucks spokesperson said: “Workers United represents approximately 5% of our US partners, and we believe actions like these divert attention from the work at the bargaining table.”

“Our partners and coffeehouses are focused on bringing the joy of the holidays to life for our customers. Based on our experience with prior similar actions, we don’t expect any meaningful disruption and look forward to serving our customers through the holidays,” a spokesperson for Starbucks wrote in an email.

The spokesperson noted that “according to independent research, Starbucks offers the best overall pay and benefits in the industry, worth on average more than $30 per hour and including comprehensive healthcare, 100% upfront tuition coverage, company stock and up to 18 weeks of paid parental leave for partners working as little as 20 hours a week, which is why our turnover is among the industry’s lowest, and nearly 3 million people applied to wear the green apron last year”.

articles.title: Home sales hit 16-year low in October amid record-high mortgage rates
articles.text:
US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by record-high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

Mortgage rates had been steadily declining in 2024 and 2025, with the 30-year rate falling below 6% for the first time in February 2026. But increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war have pushed rates back up to a nearly three-year high.

The 30-year mortgage rate, which is the most commonly used rate in home loans, is now hovering at about 7.18%, not far from its 2023 high of 7.79%. During the pandemic, average mortgage rates were just above 3%.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the NAR. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Pending home sales, or the number of contracts that have been signed before closing, reached its lowest levels in the NAR’s history in September, the same month that the 30-year mortgage rate topped 7% for the first time in nearly two years.

Mortgage rates have been directly affected by interest rate changes by the US Federal Reserve, which in September hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023. Rates currently sit at a range of 3.75% to 4%.

The central bank is poised to raise rates again next month to combat heightened inflation, which went up more than expected in October.

Affordability and cost-of-living concerns played an outsized role in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of Congress next year. According to the latest census data, growth in median rent across the US outpaced inflation. The home-ownership rate in the US has stagnated since 2021, according to the same data.

articles.title: Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus
articles.text:
Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.

Early odds suggest a Democrat may win the presidential election in two years, a fitting coda to last week’s broad rejection of the Maga brand of politics. It’s not beyond hope to expect a Democratic trifecta that will spend less time on settling grievances and more on fixing a threadbare social safety net that allows for the deepest poverty in the affluent world.

And yet, the post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money. The federal deficit is now running at about 6.2% of GDP. The federal debt hit $40tn, more than 120% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Paying interest on that debt costs some 3.2% of GDP. That’s about $1tn, more than is spent on national defense. The Congressional Budget Office projects that debt and interest payments will continue to grow faster than the economy over the coming decades. In October alone, the first month of the 2027 fiscal year, the fiscal deficit ballooned to $409bn.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that restoring the subsidies to health insurance plans under Obamacare from 2030 to 2039 would cost $460bn. Undoing the budget cuts to the Snap food stamp program and Medicaid that Trump used to partly fund the tax cuts in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would cost $2.2tn over that decade. “Reversing the harms is going to be very expensive,” said CBPP’s senior director for Federal budget policy, Brendan Duke.

And that’s the easy part. The trust fund that pays for social security benefits is scheduled to run out of money in less than six years, when the new crop of Democratic senators are still in their first term. By law, that would lead to an automatic 22% cut in benefits. Fixing that will require more money. Artificial intelligence may further complicate the picture, burdening the safety net with potentially millions of workers displaced by the new technological revolution.

Historian Bruce Bartlett, who back in the day advised Ronald Reagan on budget policy, argues that this state of affairs is the outcome of a Republican strategy honed over the years since Gipper’s day: cut taxes to strangle the budget and tie the hands of whatever Democratic administration comes next.

Trump’s OBBBA will add somewhere between $4.1tn and $5.5tn to the federal debt over 10 years, depending on whether temporary tax cuts in the bill are made permanent by a future Congress, something that has usually happened in the past. This, Bartlett once told me, will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”.

The new taxes that would be needed just to fill the holes Trump and his Republican enablers bored into the budget, let alone patch up the safety net they gleefully eviscerated, seem beyond anything achieved in recent memory.

Consider this: The last time that a government with any Republican in power delivered a tax increase was in the 1990s, when George HW Bush was president and Congress was blue. Bush paid for his sin, though, losing reelection to Democrat Bill Clinton. And that was the end of that.

Democrats have raised money when they held the presidency and Congress. But the trend suggests the opportunities are fading. Bill Clinton’s 1993 tax increases are estimated to yield the equivalent of $3.3tn over the 2030-2039 decade, adjusting for inflation. But the feat, which helped produce the nation’s first budget surplus since the 1960s, was ultimately spent on a tax cut by Clinton’s successor, George W. Bush.

The next shot at raising taxes was more modest. Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act raised the equivalent of $1.1tn over 2030-2039, in inflation-adjusted dollars. But Obama also made permanent some of George W Bush’s tax cuts. Joe Biden tried to go bigger: his original Build Back Better Act, passed in the House, would have raised the equivalent of $2.3tn over that window. But the Senate nixed that, authorizing only about $700bn in the Inflation Reduction Act.

How much more tax revenue does the US need? It depends on what Democrats want to achieve. Total tax revenue in the US amounts to less than 26% of its gross domestic product. That is 9 percentage points less than Britain’s total tax take, as a share of its economy, 9.5 points less than Canada’s, 12.5 points less than Germany’s and 16 percentage points less than Sweden’s.

Perhaps matching other rich countries is an impossibly high bar. Still, Democrats must prove that they understand the new America they hope to build comes with a price tag they are willing to fight for.

Some tax cuts in Trump’s OBBBA are set to expire in the next couple of years: exemptions on income from tips and overtime, a new deduction for seniors and an increase in the deduction for state and local taxes. The CBPP observed that these cuts offer next to nothing to Americans on the bottom rungs of the income distribution. Extending them would cost about $1.2tn over the 10-year window.

Will Democrats have the guts to end them? That will be the test of whether America is ready for a new social contract or not.

articles.title: Crystal Palace sack boss Pierre Sage after 16 games
articles.text:
Crystal Palace have sacked manager Pierre Sage after just five months in charge, with the club bottom of the Premier League.

Former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank is in advanced talks to take over.

Sunday's 3-1 defeat by Liverpool was Palace's fourth in succession in the Premier League.

The Eagles have won just two of their opening 10 games and also have the worst defensive record in the league, conceding 24 goals.

Palace are also 21st in the 36-team Europa League table, with one win from their four matches.

In a statement, the club said that three members of Sage's coaching staff - Jamal Alioui, Damien Della Santa and Sandy Guichard - had also left the club.

Palace added: "The club thanks Pierre and his staff for their efforts during their time in South London, and wish them well for the future.

"An update on the process of appointing a new manager will be provided in due course."

Sage is the second Premier League manager to be sacked this season, after Michael Carrick was also dismissed by Manchester United on Thursday.

The 47-year-old Frenchman was appointed on a three-year contract in June after Oliver Glasner departed at the end of last season.

He previously led Lens to a second-place finish in Ligue 1 and a first French Cup triumph in their 120-year history.

However, he has been unable to replicate Glasner's success at Palace. Glasner, now manager of Nottingham Forest, led Palace to a first FA Cup title and a Europa Conference League triumph.

Palace are winless in the league since 11 October and their losing run began with a 5-0 defeat by fierce rivals Brighton.

Sage said afterwards he felt "shame" from the defeat and admitted he did not know if he would be given time to turn Palace's fortunes around.

However, there was a degree of sympathy from some behind the scenes at Selhurst Park in the immediate aftermath of that loss.

Injuries were not kind to his plans, while the absence of forward players Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr - due to a mixture of fitness and personal issues related to both players' desire to leave the club - did not help.

However, three successive defeats followed, with Palace hitting the bar and having a goal ruled out in their loss to Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

Sage won five of his 16 games in all competitions.

Palace's next Premier League match is at Coventry on 21 November, after the international break.

Frank was sacked by Tottenham in February, after just under eight months in charge.

The former Brentford boss left Spurs 16th in the Premier League and five points above the relegation zone following an eight-match winless run in the league.
